h1:
Ratchaburi Cafes by the Mae Klong
10 Spots in the Old Town & Dragon Jar District
intro: Ratchaburi is known for its dragon jars, but there's more to it than that. The old town along the Mae Klong River is full of old Chinese-Portuguese shophouses, the Koyki Market, and the Tao Hong Tai kilns that have turned into an art space. Several cafes have opened up in this area, so you can sip coffee while watching the river and soaking up the dragon-jar town atmosphere all in one place. We've picked 10 spots that both locals and travelers keep talking about.

blocks.html: Ratchaburi's old town sits right on the Mae Klong River, and you can walk from the Chinese shrine and Koyki Market all the way to the National Museum in a short stretch. Many of the old shophouses have been turned into cafes and galleries, while the Tao Hong Tai kiln district has gone from firing dragon jars to becoming an art space with a coffee corner. If you like wandering an old town slowly and stopping at cafes along the way, Ratchaburi can keep you going all day.

blocks.text: Ranking the Old Town & Riverside Cafes

blocks.html: We ranked these by how well they fit the theme of “sipping coffee while taking in the dragon-jar town and the riverside.” Prices are rough ranges based on typical menu items and may shift depending on when you go. We'd recommend checking each shop's opening days before heading out, since some close mid-week.

items.name: Tao Hong Tai: d Kunst
items.blurb: An old house from the reign of King Rama V on the bank of the Mae Klong, reworked into a contemporary art gallery by the Tao Hong Tai kilns, with a coffee corner to sit at. Head up to the top-floor balcony and you'll find a Ganesha statue facing the river, with a cool breeze coming off the water. It's one spot where you get the art, the history of the dragon-jar town, and a river view all at once.
items.meta: Woradet Road, near the National Museum · open on select days

items.name: A-Tee Kopi
items.blurb: A cafe with the feel of an old-school coffee shop, decked out in vintage style like a classic local coffee hangout, on Woradet Road in the old town. It serves coffee and tea alongside breakfast bites like soft-boiled eggs, dim sum, and toast. A good place to start the morning before wandering the old town, with friendly prices.

items.name: Tara Coffee
items.blurb: A riverside cafe in the Nong Klang Na area with a deck that juts out over the water, so you can watch the river from inside or out. The menu item people keep mentioning is the stretchy cheese bread. It's a place you can linger, good for photos and an easy afternoon.
items.meta: Nong Klang Na, Mae Klong riverside · good for lingering

items.name: Saturday Sip
items.blurb: A riverside cafe that reviewers rate highly, with a cool breeze off the water. Both the coffee and the soup are menu favorites. The place isn't large but it's comfortable, and it suits anyone after a quiet corner by the river rather than a big, busy spot.

items.name: Coffee Please in the Garden
items.blurb: A leafy, green-toned riverside cafe with savory dishes, desserts, and ice cream. You can sit all day, there are photo spots in the garden, and it works well for families or groups of friends who want to settle in for a while.

items.name: Thanks
items.blurb: A riverside cafe on Tha Sao Road, looking across to a wide stretch of water, with orchids dotted around the place for an easy, restful feel. The menu covers both savory and sweet, with prices that start affordable. A nice spot to chill by the river in the evening.
items.meta: Tha Sao Road, Mae Klong riverside · good in the evening

items.name: Normal Cafe and Stay
items.blurb: A newer cafe on the Mae Klong, plain but with a sense of style, and it has accommodation on site. Good for anyone who wants a minimalist riverside cafe without the loud, photo-heavy crowds. Quiet and easy.

items.name: My Space Coffee & River
items.blurb: A riverside cafe that stands out for being shady and breezy by the water. Reviewers like the calm atmosphere, so it's a good place to escape the heat and sit down to work or read quietly by the river.
items.meta: Mae Klong riverside · good for working

items.name: SOP Café
items.blurb: A riverside cafe people talk about for its design, with a tunnel-like walkway at the entrance and a modern, minimalist interior. The river view is pretty and it suits the photo crowd. The coffee is solid rather than special, so come mainly for the atmosphere and the shots.

items.name: Quarry Haus
items.blurb: A cafe converted from an old stone-crushing mill in the Nong Ya Plong community, done up in loft style with both air-conditioned and outdoor zones. It's known for its bakery and photo spots. It isn't on the river, but the old-factory feel fits Ratchaburi's craft-town character.
items.meta: Nong Hiang area · former stone mill

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: Many of the riverside cafes are at their best in the morning or evening, since midday sun here is fairly strong and hot. If you're going specifically to shoot photos by the water, skip 11:00–14:00 for softer light and a more comfortable sit.

blocks.text: Pairing the Old Town Walk With a Cafe

blocks.html: The charm of this area is that it's walkable. The old shophouses along Woradet Road and around Koyki Market still hold onto their Chinese-Portuguese feel, from the old wooden doors and red lanterns to the vintage shop signs. Once you're done strolling and taking photos, you can drop into a cafe in the same neighborhood.

items: Koyki Market — an old market on the Mae Klong in the town center, with Chinese-Portuguese shophouses that are fun to walk and photograph
Tao Hong Tai kilns — nearly century-old dragon-jar kilns turned into an art space, with a coffee corner
Ratchaburi National Museum — sits by the Mae Klong, an easy continuation from the cafe district
Woradet Road — the old-town street lined with both traditional coffee shops and galleries

blocks.text: Cafes in the Dragon Jar District

blocks.html: The dragon jar is the symbol of Ratchaburi. Tao Hong Tai is an old kiln that still fires ceramics and has opened part of its grounds as an art space with a coffee corner. Sitting down for coffee surrounded by dragon jars and ceramic work is an atmosphere you won't find easily elsewhere. If you're into craft and art, this district is the highlight of a Ratchaburi cafe trip.

items.name: Coffee corner at Tao Hong Tai: d Kunst
items.blurb: Sip coffee in an old riverside house full of artwork, then head up to the top-floor balcony to catch the Mae Klong breeze.

items.name: Watching the dragon-jar kilns
items.blurb: Before or after coffee, walk through and see the real process of shaping and firing dragon jars in the workshop.

faq.q: Which cafes are in Ratchaburi's riverside old town?
faq.a: In the riverside old town you'll find Tao Hong Tai: d Kunst, an art gallery with a coffee corner; A-Tee Kopi, a traditional coffee shop on Woradet Road; and riverside cafes like Tara Coffee, Thanks, and Saturday Sip where you can sit and watch the water.

faq.q: Is there really a cafe inside the dragon-jar kilns?
faq.a: Yes. The Tao Hong Tai kilns have opened part of the grounds as a contemporary art space called d Kunst, set in an old house by the Mae Klong, with a coffee corner to sit at. You get the dragon-jar setting and the ceramic work at the same time.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Ratchaburi's cafes?
faq.a: Morning or evening is more comfortable, since midday sun is strong. Many of the riverside cafes get their best atmosphere and light in the early morning and around sunset. Check opening days before you go, since some close mid-week.

faq.q: Roughly how much do Ratchaburi cafes cost?
faq.a: Most coffees run around ฿50–90, while snacks and desserts are about ฿60–160. Traditional coffee shops like A-Tee Kopi are cheaper, starting in the tens of baht.

faq.q: Can you walk around Ratchaburi's old town?
faq.a: Easily. The riverside old town — including Koyki Market, Woradet Road, the Tao Hong Tai kilns, and the National Museum — is all within walking distance. You can stroll and take photos, then drop into a cafe in the same area.
